Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 404 matches in 145 texts. The retained evidence includes Linji's four-member enumeration, Linji's own transmitted answer, and three independent later question-and-answer deployments. Family revalidation against the “four selections” (四料揀), “take away the person, not the situation” (奪人不奪境), “take away both person and situation” (人境俱奪), and “take away neither person nor situation” (人境俱不奪) confirms that this is one roster member rather than an independent statement. Different answers are readings/deployments of the same category and must not be split under item 8. SenseKey remains null: Linji supplies the historical source, but the same category and meaning recur across later masters and texts, so historical origin does not make the sense master-specific.

Senses.Explanation: Taking away the environment but not the person is one member of Linji’s Four Selections, stated as a rubric and answered through fresh images. The second member of Linji's “four selections” (四料揀): literally, “take away the situation, not the person.” Here “situation” (境) is the presented surroundings or objects, while “person” (人) is the person. Linji first enumerates four possibilities in an evening instruction: sometimes take away the person but not the situation; sometimes take away the situation but not the person; sometimes take away both; sometimes take away neither. In the recorded follow-up he answers this member with, “the king's command has already gone throughout the realm; the general beyond the frontier has ended smoke and dust” (王令已行天下遍，將軍塞外絕煙塵). Later masters retain the exact category but supply different answers: “secretly transmit the emperor's edict; double the journey by a hundred stages,” “build the altar and appoint the general,” “muddy head and earthy face,” or paired states such as “silent, silent; alert, alert.” The category is therefore a reusable public-interview question within Linji's fourfold roster, not a proposition whose intent this entry resolves. Its Zen deviation lies in the bureaucratic verb “take away” becoming one axis of a named appraisal scheme for person and presented situation.

Senses.Explanation: The black dragon is the dragon beneath whose jaw the records place a brilliant pearl. In the Complete Book of the Five Lamps, Tianyi Yihuai's awakening verse speaks of seizing that pearl, and his final verse says that the dragon's horn is crushed. In the Compendium of the Five Lamps, an unnamed monk asks Dapu Xuantong how the pearl can be obtained; Dapu answers by clapping and looking sharply. Yu'an Yu later uses the black dragon's chin-pearl image while appraising the Nanyuan cat case. Wuyi Yuanlai's Extensive Record warns of mortal danger, while the Recorded Sayings of Sanyi Mingyu announces the pearl in hand. The Song of the Black Dragon's Pearl in the Zutang Collection is Danxia Tianran's named composition; it develops the pearl phrase but does not change the headword from the dragon into the pearl. Thus the dragon, its jaw, horn, and guarded pearl form one referential family, while the actions performed around them are deployments rather than extra senses.
